implementation_notes: The smell lives in a decision, not in code, so no language can express it and no tool detects it — the remedy is a process change. The mechanism is asymmetric cost salience: when a problem arrives, the acquisition cost of an alternative is visible, front-loaded and attributable, while the misfit cost of forcing the incumbent is invisible, deferred and easy to blame on the problem. The intervention is therefore to make the misfit cost visible at decision time: write the problem's requirements (throughput, latency, data shape, consistency, operating model) before naming a tool, then run a bounded spike against one alternative so the comparison is empirical. The boundary for the accusation is a parameter test, not a rule about reuse — real investment in hiring, training and vendor ties justifies some preference, and the line is where misfit cost exceeds the saved acquisition cost.
idiom_name: requirements-first decision process; spike against one alternative
code_sketch:
# the decision record that avoids the smell
requirement: 50k writes/s, 20ms p99, partition-by-tenant
candidates:   relational | document | timeseries
decision:    relational, because the query model fits; revisit if p99 > 40ms
# note: 'the team knows SQL' is not one of the requirements
pitfalls: Treating it as a ban on reuse spreads competence shallowly across tools with no depth anywhere.
Replacing familiarity with fashion is the same error with better branding.
A requirement list written after the tool is chosen will contain the tool's constraints as requirements, which is the trap the process change exists to prevent.
